title: Unitree unveils 'Superman' humanoid — 2m jump, 12.66 m/s, no hands yet
subtitle: The Hangzhou robotics firm's dynamic-movement platform lands days before its Shanghai IPO, and the specs are company claims until an independent test protocol appears.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Hangzhou-based Unitree Robotics unveiled a new humanoid platform it calls 'Superman' on August 18, 2026, days before the company's IPO on the Shanghai Stock Exchange. The company says the machine achieved a standing jump of two metres and a top running speed of 12.66 metres per second — faster over 100 metres than any recorded human sprint. Superman was developed in a little over three months, has an 0.85-metre leg length, and ships without hands or grippers. Unitree describes it as an experimental platform for highly dynamic movement, not a commercial product.

Unitree is already the world's biggest humanoid-robot maker by sales, and Superman lands the week the company is scheduled to become the first general-purpose robotics company to list on mainland China's stock market. The IPO raised 6.1 billion yuan (about $905 million). The specifications remain company claims — no third-party test protocol has been published covering surface conditions, payload, or repeatability — so the jump height and sprint speed should be treated as reported, not verified.

The launch fits a broader push by Chinese robotics firms to demonstrate hardware breakthroughs ahead of capital-market events. BYD teased its own humanoid in late July, Booster's T2 flagship reached market in July, and X Square Robot closed a $2.8 billion Series C in June. Whether any of these platforms can carry payload, manipulate objects reliably, or run for a shift alongside human coworkers is a separate question from whether they can jump — but jumping is what fits in a 30-second video and moves a stock price.

A note for learners watching the humanoid space: peak-performance demos are marketing artefacts, not deployment evidence. The useful metric for a robot that is going to work in a factory or a warehouse is mean time between failure, cycle time on a real task, and cost per operating hour — none of which appear in a highlight reel. When you see a new robot demo, the first question worth asking is what it can do for eight hours, not for eight seconds.
